description: In any sentence, the form of the verb must agree with its main subject in number and person. This is the most crucial rule for accurate sentence structure in English grammar.

sections.title: Basic Rules
sections.description: The fundamental relationship between singular and plural subjects and their corresponding verbs.

grammar_rules.structure: Singular Subject + Singular Verb | Plural Subject + Plural Verb
grammar_rules.explanation: If the subject is singular, the verb must be singular (e.g., is, was, has, plays). If the subject is plural, the verb must be plural (e.g., are, were, have, play).

key_concepts.explanation: Adding 's/es' to a noun makes it plural (e.g., Boy -> Boys), whereas adding 's/es' to a verb makes it singular (e.g., Play -> Plays).

examples.incorrect_or_context: The boy play cricket every day.
examples.correct_or_usage: The boy plays cricket every day.
examples.explanation: Here, 'boy' is a singular subject, so the verb must also be 'plays' (singular).

sections.title: Conjunctions (And, Or, Nor)
sections.description: Rules for when two or more subjects are connected by 'and', 'or', or 'nor'.

grammar_rules.structure: Subject 1 + or/nor + Subject 2 + Verb (Agrees with Subject 2)
grammar_rules.explanation: When subjects are joined by 'either...or', 'neither...nor', 'not only...but also', or simply 'or', the verb always agrees with the subject nearest to it.

examples.incorrect_or_context: Neither the manager nor the employees was present.
examples.correct_or_usage: Neither the manager nor the employees were present.
examples.explanation: The verb 'were' agrees with its nearest subject 'employees' (plural).

exceptions.condition: When two words joined by 'and' express a Single Idea.
exceptions.explanation: If two nouns joined by 'and' refer to the same person, thing, or idea, the verb used is singular.
exceptions.example: Bread and butter is my favorite breakfast.

sections.title: Intervening Words
sections.description: Additional phrases coming after the subject that can create confusion in identifying the true subject.

grammar_rules.structure: Subject 1 + (as well as / along with / with) + Subject 2 + Verb (Agrees with Subject 1)
grammar_rules.explanation: When two subjects are joined by 'as well as', 'along with', 'together with', 'in addition to', or 'besides', the verb always agrees with the first subject.

examples.incorrect_or_context: The captain, along with his players, are going to the ground.
examples.correct_or_usage: The captain, along with his players, is going to the ground.
examples.explanation: The main subject 'The captain' is singular, so 'is' is used. The phrase 'along with his players' is just additional information.

strategies.title: Identify the Main Subject
strategies.detail: In error spotting questions, mentally remove prepositional phrases or information between commas and focus solely on the main subject to check verb agreement.

sections.title: Indefinite Pronouns
sections.description: Usage of verbs with pronouns that do not refer to a specific person or thing.

key_concepts.explanation: Pronouns such as each, every, either, neither, everyone, anybody, someone, nobody, and everything are always considered singular.

examples.incorrect_or_context: Each of the students have passed the exam.
examples.correct_or_usage: Each of the students has passed the exam.
examples.explanation: The pronoun 'Each' is always singular, even if the noun following 'of the' (students) is plural.

exceptions.condition: SANAM Rule (Some, All, None, Any, Most)
exceptions.explanation: These specific pronouns take a plural verb with countable nouns and a singular verb with uncountable nouns.
exceptions.example: All of the water is gone. (Singular) | All of the students are here. (Plural)

sections.title: Collective Nouns & Fixed Amounts
sections.description: Special rules related to groups, distance, time, and money.

key_concepts.explanation: When collective nouns like jury, team, committee, or family act together as a single cohesive unit, a singular verb is used.

examples.incorrect_or_context: Fifty miles are a long distance to walk.
examples.correct_or_usage: Fifty miles is a long distance to walk.
examples.explanation: Here, 'Fifty miles' represents a fixed distance as a single unbroken unit, so the singular verb 'is' is used.

exceptions.explanation: If the members of a collective noun have differences of opinion or are acting individually instead of collectively, the verb becomes plural.
exceptions.example: The jury are divided in their opinion.
